title: Does swinging harder make you a more productive hitter?
text:
Since the beginning of the 21st century, Major League Baseball has significantly evolved. The days of reasonable financial competitiveness are gone, with teams like the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets outpricing the rest of the league. The results? Multiple lockouts over the last five years, and a cloudy outlook that baseball will even be played in 2027.
But the sport has changed in terms of analytics, too. Simply put, teams value different metrics than they used to. While batting average and counting stats used to get players paid and were viewed as the most important numbers, front offices have put more emphasis on underlying data. Exit velocity, launch angle, swing speed and barrel rate are just some of these new stats. More traditional stats like OPS (on-base plus slugging) and home runs still matter, but are often paired with new-age metrics.
The turn has created a rift in the sport, creating two types of players: those who hit the ball hard and display power, and those who don’t but get on base.
So, with this newfound emphasis on numbers that the average viewer will most likely never see, how do we determine what makes someone a good hitter? Is the answer just hitting the ball harder? Let’s dive in.
Remember when your Little League coach said you don’t have to swing too hard to hit the ball hard? That was a lie. The first thing we need to understand is that there is a correlation between swing speed and exit velocity, which is the speed the ball leaves the bat. Baseball Savant displays underlying metrics for players that show their swing speed and their exit velocity.
To show this, let’s create a scatterplot that shows where every MLB hitter fell between the two numbers in 2026. We will select five of the sport’s most unique players and determine where they fall.
Let’s take a look at how bat speed affects exit velocity.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(gt)
library(ggbeeswarm)

standard <- read_csv("data/standard_stats.csv")
savant <- read_csv("data/exit_velocity.csv")
bat_tracking <- read_csv("data/bat_tracking.csv")

bat_tracking <- bat_tracking |>
  select(id, avg_bat_speed) |>
  rename(player_id = id)
  
savant <- savant |>
  select(player_id, `last_name, first_name`, avg_hit_speed) |>
  separate(`last_name, first_name`,
           into = c("Last", "First"),
           sep = ", ") |>
  mutate(Player = case_when(
    First == "Oneil" & Last == "Cruz" ~ "Oneil Cruz",
    First == "Nick" & Last == "Kurtz" ~ "Nick Kurtz",
    First == "Junior" & Last == "Caminero" ~ "Junior Caminero",
    First == "Steven" & Last == "Kwan" ~ "Steven Kwan",
    First == "Chandler" & Last == "Simpson" ~ "Chandler Simpson",
  ))

hitting <- savant |>
 inner_join(bat_tracking)

highlighted_hitting <- hitting |>
  filter(is.na(Player) == FALSE)

ggplot(hitting, aes(x = avg_bat_speed, y = avg_hit_speed)) +
  geom_point(color = "lightgrey") +
  geom_point(
    data = highlighted_hitting,
    aes(color = Player),
    size = 3
    ) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "maroon", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = highlighted_hitting,
    aes(label = Player),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Swing Hard, Hit it Hard... right?",
    subtitle = "Players with faster bat speeds tend to hit the ball harder.",
    x = "Average Bat Speed (mph)",
    y = "Average Exit Velocity (mph)",
    color = "Highlighted Players",
    caption = "Source: Baseball Savant | By Kyler Cox"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









The most prominent name on this list is Tampa Bay Rays third baseman Junior Caminero. An All-Star in 2026, Caminero led all MLB hitters with an average bat speed of 79.4 mph. It resulted in a lot of hard contact, too. He averaged a 92.7 mph exit velocity.
Athletics first baseman Nick Kurtz and Pittsburgh Pirates center fielder Oneil Cruz are also represented on the graph. Both players were among the top five in swing speed, and both ranked in the top 10 of MLB in exit velocity.
On the other side of the chart, Cleveland Guardians outfielder Steven Kwan and Rays outfielder Chandler Simpson represent the inverse of the first three players. Kwan had the slowest bat speed in baseball (62.4), which has resulted in a bottom-five exit velocity of 83.9 mph. Simpson also fell on the slower end of swing speed (65.1) and had a bottom-three exit velocity in the sport (83.7).
But do these numbers really mean anything? Production is what really matters, and if swinging harder produces harder contact, then hard contact must produce better results, right? By looking at a beeswarm plot, we can see that there is a clear relation between OPS and harder exit velocity.


Code
standard <- standard |>
  mutate(Player = gsub("\\*", "", Player)) |>
  separate(Player, into = c("First", "Last"), sep = " ") |>
  select(First, Last, BA, OBP, SLG, HR, OPS)

exit_velo_stats <- savant |>
  inner_join(standard)

exit_velo_groups <- exit_velo_stats |>
  mutate(velo_group = case_when(
    avg_hit_speed >= 91 ~ "91+ mph",
    avg_hit_speed >= 88 ~ "88 to 91 mph",
    avg_hit_speed < 88 ~ "Under 88 mph"
  ))

highlighted_exit_velo <- exit_velo_groups |>
  filter(is.na(Player) == FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_beeswarm(
    data = exit_velo_groups,
    aes(x = reorder(velo_group, avg_hit_speed), y = OPS),
    color = "lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_beeswarm(
    data = highlighted_exit_velo,
    aes(x = reorder(velo_group, avg_hit_speed), y = OPS, color = Player),
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = highlighted_exit_velo,
    aes(x = reorder(velo_group, avg_hit_speed), y = OPS, label = Player),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hard Contact Does Pay Off",
    subtitle = "There is a clear difference in production when players hit the ball hard.",
    x = "Average Exit Velocity",
    y = "OPS",
    color = "Highlighted Players",
    caption = "Source: Baseball Savant, Baseball Reference | By Kyler Cox"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









The biggest thing this chart displays is the importance of measurable production, which is shown in the value of OPS. Among the three players with the highest exit velocities, Caminero, Kurtz and Cruz posted an OPS significantly above the league average of .719 in 2026. We can see these numbers using data from Baseball Reference.
Caminero’s high swing speed correlated to an .885 OPS, which was the highest among all five hitters. Kurtz posted an OPS just below that with .879, while Cruz was the lowest of the three with a number of .854.
The beeswarm plot shows that the majority of players with an average exit velocity over 91 mph sit around an .800 OPS. The middle plot displays players between 88 and 91 mph, with an average OPS just under .800, while most players under 88 mph fall in the .600-.750 OPS range.
By focusing on Kwan and Simpson, the plot clearly shows that their soft contact did not result in higher offensive production, at least from an OPS standpoint. Kwan posted a .731 OPS, just above league average, while Simpson’s .689 OPS was the worst of the five players represented on the chart.
While OPS is the top metric for determining player production, we still need to add other numbers into the equation to tell the whole story. Let’s do that by switching to a gt table chart.


Code
hitter_stats <- exit_velo_stats |>
  inner_join(bat_tracking)

player_comparison <- hitter_stats |>
  filter(is.na(Player) == FALSE) |>
  select(Player, avg_bat_speed, avg_hit_speed, BA, OBP, SLG, HR, OPS)

player_comparison <- player_comparison |>
  mutate(avg_bat_speed = round(avg_bat_speed, 1),
         avg_hit_speed = round(avg_hit_speed, 1),
         BA = round(BA, 3),
         OBP = round(OBP, 3),
         SLG = round(SLG, 3),
         OPS = round(OPS, 3))

player_comparison <- player_comparison |>
  rename(`Average Bat Speed` = avg_bat_speed,
         `Average Exit Velocity` = avg_hit_speed,
         `Batting Average` = BA,
         `On-Base Percentage` = OBP,
         `Slugging Percentage` = SLG,
         `Home Runs` = HR)

player_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(`Average Bat Speed`)) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "So Swinging Hard Does Matter...",
    subtitle = "Players who swing harder produce more home runs and a higher OPS, and it's not close:"
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Player = "Player",
    `Average Bat Speed` = "Swing Speed",
    `Average Exit Velocity` = "Exit Velo",
    `Batting Average` = "BA",
    `On-Base Percentage` = "OBP",
    `Slugging Percentage` = "SLG",
    `Home Runs` = "HR",
    OPS = "OPS"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Average Bat Speed`, `Average Exit Velocity`),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Batting Average`, `On-Base Percentage`,
                `Slugging Percentage`, OPS),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(
      cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
      cell_text(weight = "bold", size = 14)
    )
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Player)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#F4C7C3"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = Player == "Junior Caminero")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "lightblue"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = Player == "Steven Kwan")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Baseball Savant, Baseball Reference | By Kyler Cox"
  )

This chart reinforces what we already knew: that hitting the ball harder generates more offensive production. This can be seen by adding batting average, on-base percentage, slugging percentage and home runs to the equation.
Caminero is the best hitter on the list. His swing speed leads the group, as do his .524 slugging percentage and 42 home runs. Kurtz and Cruz are not far behind, with their high swing speeds translating into the top-two exit velocities. All three hitters have an exit velocity over 92 mph, and all three have at least 20 home runs and at least an .850 OPS.
Kwan and Simpson fall to the bottom of the list in home runs and slugging percentage. There is a caveat, though, in that Kwan has the second-highest on-base percentage of the group (.382) and the second-highest batting average (.282). Simpson leads the group in batting average, hitting .306 in 2026.
This suggests more complete at-bats, but it does not make up for their lost production in OPS, which ranges over .100 points below the top three hitters. The difference in Caminero’s 42 home runs, to Simpson’s zero, is more significant than just the .030 batting average difference between the two hitters. The same can be said about Kwan’s on-base percentage, which is .014 points higher than Cruz’s (.368), even though Cruz has 17 more home runs than Kwan.
Hitting the ball harder does make you a better, more productive hitter. The numbers point toward this. And as long as baseball continues to prioritize underlying metrics, MLB’s best players will continue to be those who swing hard, hit hard and produce more.
